title: Fortresses: when more material cannot break through
outcomes: Names what a queen-against-rook-and-pawn fortress needs: covered entry squares, protected pieces and a safe waiting move
Predicts, for one-feature changes, whether a fortress holds or breaks
Tests a claimed fortress by looking for the break before relying on it

steps.text: A **fortress** is a set-up that the stronger side cannot break, even with extra material. The weaker side keeps its pieces protecting one another, covers the squares the enemy could enter, and keeps a harmless waiting move. For the best-known case, a wrong-coloured bishop with a rook pawn, see the lesson *The wrong bishop: a rook pawn that cannot win*.

steps.caption: Black to move: king, rook and a pawn against a queen. Natural moves such as Ra5 and Rc6 lose; Rb6 holds. The tablebase says the position is a draw; one line is shown.

line.say: The queen checks on the a-file.

claims.statement: With Black to move, the result is a draw.

steps.text: **Ask three questions.** (1) Is every square the queen could enter, or check from, covered? (2) Do the defenders protect each other, and is none forced to move away? (3) Is there a waiting move that breaks nothing? Rule of thumb: the set-up fails if some defender is attacked more often than it is protected, or if the stronger side can force a defender off its post so that an entry square is uncovered.

steps.title: One square less
steps.prompt: Black has a king, a rook and an f-pawn against a queen. In the second position the black king stands on e8 instead of f8. In the third only the white king has moved. Predict each result, then check.
Which of the three questions did you ask first? In a position where the stronger side won, which question would have shown you the break?
